hook_text: Too many diamonds is a problem. Here is how one company solved it.
clip_script: Kimberley, 1871. The diggers make a rule: one man, one claim. Everyone gets a small square and a fair shot. But diamonds pour out of the ground, more than the world has ever seen, and prices crash. Producing more only makes it worse. The mine goes deep, rocks fall, water floods in, and the claim limit is scrapped. Companies buy everything. By 1888 one company, De Beers, owns almost every mine. Now it can do what no digger could: turn down the tap. Fewer diamonds dug. Extra stones locked away. From 1890 a group of London merchants releases them slowly. Prices climb back up. Owners get rich. Workers in compounds stay poor. A diamond is valuable because someone makes sure it stays rare.
visual_style: A whiteboard grid of claims merging into one big square, then a giant tap over a basket of diamonds being turned down to a trickle, with a price arrow rising.
pacing: Fast crash, a pause, then a slow controlled drip.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see how the price of diamonds was made.
